title: Jerome in Bethlehem (c. 347–420)
hookLine: a prickly scholar translates the Bible into everyday Latin

cards: A young scholar falls sick with a fever, and dreams he's dragged before the judgment seat. A voice asks who he is. A Christian, he answers.
You lie, says the voice. Ciceronianus es, non Christianus. You're a Ciceronian, not a Christian.
The scholar is Jerome, and he tells this dream himself in a letter. He loved Cicero's polished Latin and found the plain style of the Bible hard to stomach.
Strange, then, that this is the man who spent his later years in Bethlehem putting the Bible into plain Latin for ordinary churchgoers.

teach.b: First, the man. Jerome's letters show a brilliant, restless, sharp-tongued scholar, warm with friends and fierce with opponents. Holiness, in his case, didn't come with a soft personality.
Second, the problem he was asked to fix.
Latin-speaking Christians had Bibles, but the old Latin versions differed from copy to copy. A pope asked Jerome to revise the Gospels, and the work grew from there. Third, the bold step.

teach.h: BACK TO THE HEBREW, IN BETHLEHEM.
teach.b: For the Old Testament, Jerome went back behind the Greek to the Hebrew. In Bethlehem he worked at it, and he says he learned Hebrew from a Jewish teacher who came to him by night. Not everyone was pleased.
Augustine wrote to him, worried that a new wording in the book of Jonah had upset a congregation that knew the old one by heart. Familiar words are hard to give up. Fourth, what it became.
His translation, along with other parts of the old Latin, came to be called the Vulgate.
And here's the thread that reaches you: the Douay-Rheims, the English Bible quoted on this path, was translated from Jerome's Latin.
So when you hear "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God," you're hearing Jerome, one step removed.
In his Latin: In principio erat Verbum. The common tongue, for the common church.

how: Catholics honor Saint Jerome as a Doctor of the Church and a patron of translators and scripture scholars, and the Douay-Rheims English Bible was translated from the Latin Vulgate.

games.q: you're Jerome. the Latin copies of the Old Testament differ, and they were made from Greek. what do you translate from?
o: learn Hebrew and go back to the Hebrew.
games.why: he learned Hebrew from a Jewish teacher and translated from it, which upset some readers used to the old wording.

practice: Say the first line of John's Gospel in Jerome's Latin, slowly, even if you've never studied Latin: In principio erat Verbum. In the beginning was the Word.

Say the Latin once more and notice which words you can already guess, principio, beginning, verbum, word, or say the verse in another language you speak at home, and let the strange sound slow you down; if you pray, rest on that one line.

wordCard.voice: Vulgate. Jerome's Latin Bible, revised from the Greek and, in Bethlehem, translated from the Hebrew, for ordinary Latin-speaking churches. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the name later given to the Bible in Jerome's Latin.

carryVoice: Your line: the common tongue. Familiar words can slide past; foreign ones make you listen. Day seven hundred forty-one.
